title: One Nation, One Shepherd, One Sanctuary
summary: After the vision of the dry bones (37:1–14) and the sign of the two sticks (37:15–20), God promises to gather Israel from the nations into its own land, make Judah and Ephraim one nation under one king, 'my servant David', cleanse them from idolatry, make an everlasting covenant of peace, and set his sanctuary among them forever, so that the nations will know the LORD sanctifies Israel.
keyIssue: Is this a promise of a future national, territorial restoration of ethnic Israel under the Messiah, or is it fulfilled in Christ (the Davidic shepherd) and his one new-covenant people, as the New Testament's reuse of 37:27 in 2 Corinthians 6:16 and Revelation 21:3 suggests?

readings.reading: A literal promise to the physical descendants of Jacob: regathering to the land God gave Jacob (37:25), national reunification, and the reign of the Messiah, David's greater Son, from Jerusalem during the millennium. Many dispensationalists see the modern return to the land (1948 onward) as a preparatory, still-unbelieving stage (compare the bones assembling before breath enters, 37:7–10), with spiritual regeneration to follow at Christ's return.
readings.support: The text is concrete and geographical ('the land I gave to my servant Jacob, where your fathers lived'), and the promise is called unconditional and everlasting (37:25–26). A consistent grammatical-historical reading, it is argued, should not transfer promises made to Israel to a different referent.
readings.objection: Critics reply that the New Testament itself applies the covenant formula of 37:27 to the mixed Jewish-Gentile church (2 Corinthians 6:16) and the 'one shepherd' theme to Jesus gathering 'other sheep' (John 10:16), indicating that the apostles read the passage as fulfilled in Christ. Dispensationalists answer that an application to the church does not exhaust the original promise to Israel.

readings.reading: The promise is fulfilled in Jesus, the true David and good shepherd, who gathers one flock from Israel and the nations; the 'sanctuary among them' is God's dwelling in Christ and the church as temple, consummated in the new creation where 'the dwelling of God is with man' (Revelation 21:3). Land promises expand to the renewed earth (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5).
readings.support: The New Testament reuses this very passage for the church (2 Corinthians 6:16) and for the final state (Revelation 21:3); Jesus identifies himself as the one shepherd (John 10:11–16); Ephesians 2:14–22 describes the uniting of divided peoples into one temple.
readings.objection: Dispensationalists object that this is replacement theology that empties the 'David', 'land' and 'Judah and Ephraim' particulars of meaning. Amillennialists respond that fulfilment in Christ is not replacement but escalation: believing Israel is the root of the one people, and the promises are kept 'in a more glorious way'.

readings.reading: Agrees that the passage is fulfilled in Christ and his church, but many postmillennialists (following the Puritan hope) add that Romans 11 predicts a large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews within history, which will be a striking instance of the 'one flock' and help usher in a period of gospel blessing among the nations.
readings.support: Romans 11:12, 15, 25–26 links Israel's 'fullness' to 'life from the dead' for the world; the Puritan and Princeton tradition read Ezekiel's restoration through that lens.
readings.objection: Amillennialists counter that 'all Israel' in Romans 11:26 may be the elect remnant across the age, not a future mass conversion; dispensationalists object that conversion without land restoration still spiritualizes 37:25.

readings.reading: Historic premillennialists are divided. Ladd held that the New Testament reinterprets Old Testament Israel promises in the church, while others in the tradition expect a future turning of ethnic Israel and see a partial earthly fulfilment in Christ's millennial reign before the eternal state brings the 'everlasting' aspects to completion.
readings.support: The two-stage hope (millennium, then new creation) gives room for both an earthly reign of the Davidic king (Revelation 20) and an everlasting sanctuary (Revelation 21:3).
readings.objection: Dispensationalists think Ladd conceded too much; amillennialists think inserting a millennium adds a stage the passage does not require.

readings.reading: Jesus is the true Israel and Davidic king; the promise is fulfilled typologically in him and in all united to him, Jew and Gentile alike. The land functions as a type of the whole new creation, so the 'everlasting' land promise is kept in the renewed cosmos rather than in a territorial restoration in the present age.
readings.support: Reads Ezekiel 37 along the canonical storyline of the covenants, in which Christ fulfils Israel's vocation and the new covenant forms one people (Ephesians 2:11–22; Hebrews 8).
readings.objection: Dispensational critics say typology is used to override the plain sense of the text; covenant theologians say the view underplays continuity with the believing Israel of old.

title: Ezekiel's Temple Vision and the River of Life
summary: In 573 BC Ezekiel is taken in visions to a very high mountain and shown, by a man with a measuring line, a vast temple complex (chs. 40–43), the return of God's glory, regulations for priests, a prince, offerings and festivals (chs. 44–46), a life-giving river flowing from the temple that grows from ankle-deep to an uncrossable torrent and heals the Dead Sea (47:1–12), and a new allotment of the land around a city named 'The LORD Is There' (48:35).
keyIssue: Is this a blueprint for a literal future temple with sacrifices (a millennial temple), or a symbolic vision of restored worship fulfilled in Christ, the church and the new creation? The renewed sin and atonement offerings (43:19–27; 45:15–17) are the crux, in light of Hebrews 9–10.

readings.reading: A real temple to be built in Jerusalem for the millennial kingdom, from which Christ reigns. Older dispensationalists took the sacrifices as memorials of the cross, as the Lord's Supper is now; more recent writers (e.g. Hullinger) argue they provide ceremonial purification so that the holy presence of God can dwell among mortal, sinful people, without adding to Christ's atoning work.
readings.support: The vision supplies exact measurements, named gates, priestly divisions and tribal boundaries; such detail, it is argued, makes little sense as mere symbol. Isaiah 56:6–7, 60:7 and Zechariah 14:16–21 also envisage worship and offerings among the nations in the age to come.
readings.objection: Critics note that 45:15–17 says the offerings 'make atonement', which seems to clash with Hebrews 10:18 ('no longer any offering for sin'). Proponents answer that the Levitical sacrifices never removed sin either (Hebrews 10:4) but dealt with ritual purity, and that the same will be true of millennial sacrifices.

readings.reading: An apocalyptic-symbolic vision of the restored presence of God, fulfilled in Christ, who is the true temple (John 2:19–21), in the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21), and finally in the new Jerusalem, which has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple (Revelation 21:22). The river of 47:1–12 reappears in Revelation 22:1–2 and in Jesus's promise of living water (John 7:37–39).
readings.support: Revelation 21–22 deliberately reworks Ezekiel 40–48 (measuring, the high mountain, twelve gates, the river and trees whose leaves heal); the symmetrical dimensions and perfect square suggest an idealized vision; Hebrews forbids a return to the shadows.
readings.objection: Dispensationalists respond that symbolic readings cannot explain why so much non-symbolic detail is given, and that John's use of Ezekiel does not mean Ezekiel had nothing literal in view.

readings.reading: Shares the symbolic-fulfilment reading, but stresses the river of chapter 47 as a picture of the gospel's progressive growth in history: it deepens stage by stage until it fills the land and heals the Dead Sea, so the kingdom flowing from Christ's temple will gradually bring life to the nations before the end.
readings.support: The ever-deepening river matches the growth parables of Matthew 13:31–33 and the stone becoming a mountain (Daniel 2:35); the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:2) is taken as a process now under way.
readings.objection: Amillennialists caution that Revelation 22 places the river in the consummated new creation, not in pre-consummation history; dispensationalists hold that the river is geographically real (Zechariah 14:8).

readings.reading: An idealized theological portrait of perfected worship that was never meant to be built: Ezekiel is shown what God's dwelling among a holy people must be, with access, holiness and life spreading outward. Some add that it held out a conditional pattern for the exiles (43:10–11), which they failed to implement, and that its permanent truth is realized in Christ and the new creation.
readings.support: Ezekiel receives no command to build (contrast Exodus 25:9); the dimensions are schematic; the land allotment ignores real geography; Block reads chs. 40–48 as a theological 'constitution' for restored Israel rather than a construction plan.
readings.objection: Literal interpreters reply that 'never meant to be built' makes much of the detail pointless; others note that the conditional view raises the question why the returnees did not adopt it.

readings.reading: Historic premillennialists vary: many follow a typological reading fulfilled in Christ and the new creation, while some allow that elements may have a literal expression in Christ's millennial reign, though without the restoration of atoning sacrifices.
readings.support: The historic-premillennial tradition does not rest its case on Old Testament temple prophecies but on Revelation 20, so it can read Ezekiel 40–48 with the typological tools of New Testament usage.
readings.objection: Dispensationalists see this as inconsistent: a literal millennium in Revelation 20 but a symbolic temple in Ezekiel. Amillennialists say a symbolic Ezekiel removes a main support for an earthly interregnum.

title: They Will Look on Me, the One They Have Pierced
summary: In a section where the LORD defends Jerusalem against the nations (12:1–9), he promises to pour out on the house of David and Jerusalem a 'spirit of grace and supplication', so that they look on the one they pierced and mourn as for an only son, a mourning compared to that at Hadad-rimmon (12:11), followed by a fountain opened for cleansing from sin (13:1).
keyIssue: When and how does this mourning happen? John 19:37 applies the verse to the crucifixion and Revelation 1:7 to a coming with the clouds. Is it fulfilled at the cross and Pentecost, at AD 70, or in a future national repentance of Israel at the Second Coming?

readings.reading: A future national repentance of Israel at the close of the Tribulation: as the nations besiege Jerusalem (12:2–9; 14:1–3), the surviving Jewish people recognize Jesus as the Messiah they rejected, mourn, and are cleansed (13:1), and Christ returns to deliver them. Some teachers make this national confession the trigger for the Second Coming (compare Hosea 5:15; Matthew 23:39).
readings.support: The setting is military and national (Jerusalem, the house of David, clan by clan, 12:12–14); it parallels Romans 11:26 ('all Israel will be saved') and Matthew 24:30, where the 'tribes' mourn when they see the Son of Man.
readings.objection: Critics point out that John 19:37 already treats the piercing as fulfilled at Calvary and that Acts 2:37–41 records Jerusalem's 'cut to the heart' repentance at Pentecost. Dispensationalists reply that the piercing was fulfilled at the cross while the national looking and mourning remain future.

readings.reading: The piercing is fulfilled at the crucifixion (John 19:37); the outpoured Spirit of grace and the repentance of Jerusalem's people begin at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, 37–38), and the fountain for cleansing is Christ's atoning work. Revelation 1:7 widens the circle to 'all the tribes of the earth', who will mourn at Christ's final, visible return.
readings.support: The New Testament's two citations bracket the age: the cross (John 19:37) and the consummation (Revelation 1:7). Peter's Pentecost sermon matches the elements of 12:10 (outpoured Spirit, guilt for the crucified one, mourning, cleansing in baptism).
readings.objection: Dispensationalists object that Pentecost involved thousands, not the house of David 'clan by clan'; postmillennialists add that Romans 11 still anticipates a broader turning of Israel.

readings.reading: Fulfilled initially at the cross and Pentecost, and to be fulfilled more fully when the Spirit brings a widespread conversion of the Jewish people within history, as the Puritans expected from Romans 11; this conversion will be a great blessing to the world.
readings.support: Romans 11:12, 15 promises greater riches for the world through Israel's 'fullness'; the Spirit-wrought repentance of 12:10 fits a revival, not a coercive event at the Parousia.
readings.objection: Amillennialists question whether Romans 11 teaches a future mass conversion; dispensationalists argue the passage's battle setting points to the end of history, not a gradual revival.

readings.reading: Revelation 1:7, which combines Daniel 7:13 with Zechariah 12:10, describes Christ's 'coming in clouds' of judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70: 'those who pierced him' are the first-century generation, and the 'tribes of the land' (Greek gē can mean land) are the clans of Judea mourning their judgment.
readings.support: Revelation's time markers ('soon', 1:1; 'near', 1:3) and Jesus's warning to the high priest that he would 'see' the Son of Man coming (Matthew 26:64) fit a first-century audience; Zechariah 12:12–14 itself speaks of Israelite clans.
readings.objection: Critics note that in Zechariah 12 the mourning is repentance granted by grace and Jerusalem is defended, not destroyed, so AD 70 is an odd fulfilment; Thomas Ice presses this point. Preterists respond that Revelation 1:7 reapplies Zechariah's imagery, and that mourning can be lament under judgment as well as repentance.

readings.reading: Both the looking and the coming of Revelation 1:7 were completed in AD 70, when Christ came in the Father's glory and judged the generation that pierced him; there is no further visible coming to await.
readings.support: Takes the time texts of Revelation and Matthew 26:64 as strictly limiting the fulfilment to the first-century generation.
readings.objection: This reading denies a future visible return, placing it outside the historic creeds (Nicene Creed, 'he will come again in glory'); critics also note Revelation 1:7 says 'every eye' will see him. Proponents answer that 'every eye' is idiomatic for those involved, as in Matthew 26:64.

readings.reading: Agrees that the piercing was fulfilled at Calvary but expects a future spiritual turning of Israel at or just before Christ's return, linked to Romans 11:26 and followed by Christ's earthly reign.
readings.support: Holds together John 19:37, Revelation 1:7 and Romans 11 without requiring a pretribulational framework.
readings.objection: Amillennialists question the future mass-conversion premise; dispensationalists see the historic-premillennial treatment of Israel as underdeveloped.

title: The Day of the LORD on the Mount of Olives
summary: All nations gather to battle against Jerusalem; the city is taken and half its people exiled (14:1–2). Then the LORD goes out to fight; his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, which splits east and west (14:3–5). A unique day follows, living waters flow from Jerusalem east and west, the LORD becomes king over all the earth, and Jerusalem dwells securely (14:6–11). Later verses (14:16–21) have survivors of the nations going up yearly to keep the Feast of Booths.
keyIssue: Is this a literal end-time battle and topographical change at Christ's return before an earthly millennium, a symbolic portrait of God's victory fulfilled in Christ and the church, or a picture partly fulfilled in the Roman siege of AD 70 and the gospel's spread from Jerusalem?

readings.reading: A future siege of Jerusalem at the end of the Tribulation (Armageddon), ended by Christ's bodily return to the Mount of Olives (compare Acts 1:11–12), a real earthquake reshaping the land, and the start of his millennial reign. Because the nations who refuse to keep the Feast of Booths are punished (14:16–19), sin and death still exist: this cannot be the eternal state, so it must be the millennium.
readings.support: The geographic precision (Mount of Olives 'east of Jerusalem', specific gates and towers, 14:10), the link with Acts 1:11–12, and the presence of disobedience after the Lord becomes king all support an earthly interregnum.
readings.objection: Non-dispensationalists answer that prophetic idiom (compare Micah 1:3–4) often uses mountains splitting for theophany, and that the reinstated Feast of Booths with temple vessels and cooking pots (14:20–21) is the language of Israel's worship used for a reality the New Testament fulfils in Christ.

readings.reading: An apocalyptic picture of the decisive victory of God over the nations and the universal reign of the LORD, fulfilled in Christ's first coming, the outpouring of the Spirit (the 'living waters' of 14:8, compare John 7:37–39 and Ezekiel 47), the ingathering of the nations into the worship of God, and the final consummation where night ceases (14:7; Revelation 22:5).
readings.support: Revelation picks up Zechariah 14's motifs (no night, light from God, living water, 'no longer any curse', 14:11; Revelation 22:3) for the new creation; the 'holy to the LORD' inscription spread to ordinary pots (14:20–21) signals the end of the sacred-common distinction realized in Christ.
readings.objection: Dispensationalists object that the 'symbolic' reading is selective, conceding the literal Mount of Olives in Acts 1 while denying it here; they also ask how the eternal state can contain nations that refuse to worship (14:17).

readings.reading: Verses 1–2 describe Rome's siege and capture of Jerusalem in AD 70, a 'day of the LORD' in which God used the nations to judge the city; the LORD's going out and the waters flowing from Jerusalem are the gospel's advance from Jerusalem to the nations (Acts 1:8), and the Lord's universal kingship is Christ's present reign.
readings.support: Jesus's Olivet prophecy (spoken on the Mount of Olives) echoes the capture, the plundering and flight of 14:2–5 (Luke 21:20–24), and Acts 1–2 begins the outflow from Jerusalem.
readings.objection: Ice argues that Zechariah 14 shows the LORD rescuing Jerusalem and fighting against its attackers, the reverse of AD 70; preterists answer that 14:1–2 is judgment on the city and 14:3ff. the vindication of the faithful remnant and church, who fled and survived (Luke 21:21).

readings.reading: Emphasizes 14:9 ('the LORD will be king over all the earth') and 14:16–21 as a progressive historical triumph: through the gospel, the nations increasingly come to worship the true God, and the whole of life becomes 'holy to the LORD' before Christ's final return.
readings.support: Coheres with Psalm 22:27–28, Isaiah 2:2–4 and the growth parables; the 'holiness' inscribed on bells and cooking pots pictures the sanctification of culture.
readings.objection: Amillennialists respond that the passage's full realization is the consummated new creation, not pre-Parousia history; dispensationalists object that Christ's personal presence on the Mount of Olives (14:4) precedes the universal reign.

readings.reading: A future event at Christ's return, which inaugurates his millennial reign over the nations; the details may be literal or a mixture of literal and symbolic, but the sequence of coming, victory and a reign with remaining disobedience fits Revelation 19–20.
readings.support: Like dispensationalists, historic premillennialists find 14:16–19 hard to fit into either the present age or the eternal state.
readings.objection: Amillennialists say the passage portrays one final victory, not two stages; partial preterists see 14:1–2 as AD 70.

title: Wheat and Tares, Mustard Seed and Leaven
summary: Jesus gives three kingdom parables: an enemy sows weeds (zizania, probably darnel) among wheat, and the owner lets both grow until the harvest, when the weeds are burned and the wheat gathered (13:24–30, explained in 13:36–43 as the judgment at 'the end of the age', synteleia tou aiōnos); a mustard seed, smallest of seeds, becomes a tree in which birds nest (13:31–32); and a little leaven works through three measures of flour until all is leavened (13:33).
keyIssue: What do the parables teach about the kingdom between the two comings: steady growth to world-wide influence, a mixed field with good and evil coexisting until the end, or a 'mystery form' of the kingdom that includes corruption? And is 'the end of the age' the final judgment or the end of the Jewish age in AD 70?

readings.reading: The mustard seed and leaven promise that Christ's kingdom, though tiny in its beginnings, will grow extensively (filling the world, Daniel 2:35) and intensively (permeating every sphere of life) through the gospel before the harvest at Christ's return. The wheat and tares show the kingdom advancing in a world where evil persists until the end, but not that evil keeps pace with it.
readings.support: Leaven works 'until all was leavened' (13:33), a picture of total permeation; birds nesting in branches echoes Daniel 4:12 and Ezekiel 17:23, where nations find shelter under a great kingdom.
readings.objection: Amillennialists answer that the parables stress the contrast of small beginning and large ending, not a timetable or a dominant majority in history; dispensationalists say leaven is consistently a symbol of evil (Matthew 16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Postmillennialists reply that context, not a fixed code, decides a symbol's meaning, and Jesus says the kingdom itself is like leaven.

readings.reading: The kingdom is truly present and growing through the church age, but it grows in a world where the enemy's sowing continues side by side until the harvest; the age ends with a single judgment separating righteous and wicked. No pre-consummation golden age is promised: the kingdom's triumph is real but hidden, and its full manifestation awaits Christ's return.
readings.support: Wheat and weeds grow together 'until the harvest' (13:30), and the harvest is 'the end of the age' with one judgment of both groups (13:40–43), leaving no room for a millennium in between or a near-total eradication of evil before the end.
readings.objection: Postmillennialists say that 'coexistence' does not exclude 'proportion': the wheat can vastly outnumber the weeds. Premillennialists say a single harvest scene does not rule out an intervening kingdom phase revealed elsewhere (Revelation 20).

readings.reading: These parables describe the 'mystery form' of the kingdom during the interadvent age, after Israel's rejection of the King and before the millennial kingdom. Classic dispensationalists (e.g. Scofield, Pentecost) read the abnormally large mustard plant with birds (compare 13:4, 19, where birds are the evil one) and the leaven as pictures of corruption entering Christendom, so the age ends in apostasy rather than global conversion.
readings.support: Jesus speaks of 'the mysteries of the kingdom' (13:11), suggesting something previously unrevealed; elsewhere in Matthew leaven means false teaching (16:6, 12), and the birds in this same chapter are agents of Satan.
readings.objection: Critics note that 13:33 says 'the kingdom of heaven is like leaven', making leaven a positive figure for the kingdom itself; and a mustard 'tree' with nesting birds echoes positive Old Testament imagery of nations finding shelter. Some progressive dispensationalists accept this and read the parables as growth parables.

readings.reading: Ladd's 'mystery of the kingdom': God's reign has entered history in a hidden, unexpected form, working secretly like seed and leaven without overpowering evil; it will be manifested in power at the Parousia, followed by the millennium and the age to come.
readings.support: Explains why the kingdom foretold in Daniel 2 came first as a small, resistible presence rather than a world-crushing stone, and keeps both present reality and future consummation.
readings.objection: Postmillennialists say Ladd underplays the growth and final world-filling scope of the images; amillennialists see no need for the millennium Ladd adds after the harvest.

readings.reading: Partial preterists divide. Many (e.g. Gentry) read the harvest at 'the end of the age' as the final judgment; others (e.g. DeMar) note that synteleia tou aiōnos echoes the disciples' question in 24:3 and can denote the close of the old covenant age in AD 70, with the growth parables describing the kingdom's spread after that decisive judgment.
readings.support: Matthew uses the same phrase in 24:3, which many link to the temple's destruction; Hebrews 9:26 places Christ's appearing 'at the end of the ages'.
readings.objection: Critics reply that 13:41–43 involves angels removing all lawbreakers and the righteous shining in the Father's kingdom, which fits final judgment better than AD 70; this is why many partial preterists, and all creedal readers, keep it future.

readings.reading: The harvest at the end of the age was the AD 70 judgment ending the Mosaic age, when the 'sons of the kingdom' who rejected Christ were cast out and the righteous shone in the established kingdom; the kingdom continues to grow after that point.
readings.support: Holds 13:39–40 and 24:3 to the same 'end of the age', which Jesus placed within his generation (24:34).
readings.objection: This view denies a future final judgment at Christ's return, placing it outside historic creedal orthodoxy (Westminster Confession 33); critics also note the universal scope of 'all causes of sin and all lawbreakers' (13:41). Proponents answer that the creeds must yield to Scripture's time statements.

title: The Great Commission
summary: The risen Jesus declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (echoing Daniel 7:14), commands the eleven to 'make disciples of all nations' (panta ta ethnē), baptizing and teaching them to observe all he commanded, and promises to be with them always, 'to the end of the age' (synteleia tou aiōnos).
keyIssue: Does the commission imply its own success, the discipling of nations as nations so that the world is largely Christianized before Christ returns, or does it command a faithful worldwide witness that gathers a people from every nation while the world remains mixed or worsens?

readings.reading: The commission rests on Christ's universal authority (Daniel 7:13–14 fulfilled at his resurrection and ascension) and therefore implies its own accomplishment: whole nations will be discipled, baptized and taught to obey Christ, with his presence guaranteeing the result. History will see the gospel's widespread triumph before 'the end of the age'.
readings.support: The command is grounded in authority already possessed, not in a hoped-for future; 'make disciples of all nations' is more than 'preach to'; Psalm 2:8 and 22:27, Isaiah 2:2–4 and Daniel 2:35 promise global success.
readings.objection: Amillennialists answer that a command does not predict its degree of success, and Jesus elsewhere forecasts persecution and lawlessness (Matthew 24:9–12). Postmillennialists reply that these warnings refer largely to the pre-70 generation, and that Christ's authority makes defeat of the commission unthinkable.

readings.reading: The commission will certainly be fulfilled in the sense God intends: a people is gathered from every nation (Revelation 5:9; 7:9) and Christ is present with his church until the end of the age, his final return. It does not promise that a majority of the world will be converted; faithful witness under suffering continues alongside the growth of opposition.
readings.support: 'All nations' in Matthew typically means peoples from every nation (24:14; 25:32); the age ends with both wheat and weeds present (13:30); the New Testament expects tribulation for the church throughout the age (John 16:33; Acts 14:22).
readings.objection: Postmillennialists say this reduces Christ's universal authority to a remnant-gathering task; amillennialists answer that the gathering of a countless multitude from every tribe is no small victory and that God's sovereignty does not require statistical majorities.

readings.reading: The mandate of the church age is world evangelization and the calling out of a people for Christ's name (Acts 15:14), not the Christianization of nations. The age ends in apostasy and the Tribulation; the nations are judged and the kingdom established by Christ himself at his return (Matthew 25:31–46).
readings.support: 2 Timothy 3:1–5, 2 Thessalonians 2:3 and Luke 18:8 forecast decline; Christ, not the church, establishes the visible kingdom.
readings.objection: Postmillennialists object that this pessimism reads the commission's grounding in Christ's present authority too lightly; amillennialists agree that the commission is evangelistic but deny a separate church-age parenthesis.

readings.reading: The church proclaims the gospel to all nations as a witness (Matthew 24:14), a task that is itself a sign of the end and must be completed before Christ returns to establish his millennial reign; the kingdom's present power operates in mission, but its consummation awaits the Parousia.
readings.support: Ladd stressed that the church's mission is the means by which God's reign advances now, giving missionary urgency without promising a Christianized world.
readings.objection: Postmillennialists say Ladd's 'witness' framing understates the command to disciple nations; amillennialists accept most of the reading but not the millennium.

readings.reading: Many full preterists hold that the universal-preaching benchmark (Matthew 24:14) was met before AD 70 (Colossians 1:6, 23; Romans 10:18), and that 'the end of the age' was the close of the Mosaic age at that time. Most still regard evangelism as an ongoing duty in the endless new covenant age; a minority question whether the commission as such binds the church today.
readings.support: Paul's statements that the gospel had gone to 'all creation under heaven' (Colossians 1:23) are taken as signalling that the end of 24:14 arrived in that generation.
readings.objection: Critics argue that the promise 'I am with you always' and the command to disciple all nations hardly expired in AD 70, and that Paul's language is hyperbolic or representative; full preterism's denial of a future Second Coming also places it outside the historic creeds.

title: Before You Finish the Cities of Israel
summary: Sending the Twelve on mission, Jesus warns of persecution and says that when they are persecuted in one town they should flee to the next, for they 'will not have gone through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes'.
keyIssue: What 'coming' of the Son of Man fits a timeframe shorter than completing a mission to Israel's towns? Albert Schweitzer made the verse the cornerstone of his view that Jesus mistakenly expected the end during the disciples' first tour.

readings.reading: The coming is Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70: the disciples' mission to Israel would not be completed before the Son of Man came, as Daniel 7 foretold, to vindicate himself and end the old order. The persecution described (synagogue floggings, governors and kings, 10:17–18) fits the apostolic generation in Acts.
readings.support: The time limit is real and short; 10:17–22 reaches beyond the first tour to the whole period of apostolic witness; Matthew 16:28 and 24:34 place a 'coming' within the generation.
readings.objection: Critics ask why a 'coming' in Roman armies is called the Son of Man's coming; preterists answer that the Old Testament speaks of the LORD 'coming on the clouds' in historical judgments (Isaiah 19:1). Others argue the mission to Israel was hardly 'not completed' by AD 70 in any meaningful sense.

readings.reading: The verse refers to the one Parousia of Christ, which occurred in AD 70 within the lifetime of those addressed. Russell and later preterists cite it as evidence that the New Testament expected one coming only, in that generation.
readings.support: Matthew elsewhere uses 'the coming of the Son of Man' for the Parousia (24:27, 37, 39); the time limit is strict.
readings.objection: Denying a future bodily return places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy; critics also note that the New Testament describes the Second Coming as visible and universal (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

readings.reading: Many Reformed interpreters see a 'coming' in the vindication events that follow the cross: Jesus's resurrection and enthronement (28:18), the gift of the Spirit, and the judgment of AD 70 as stages of the one coming of the Son of Man to receive the kingdom, which is consummated at his final return.
readings.support: Ridderbos's 'fulfilment in stages' explains why the Gospels attach both near and far time markers to the Son of Man's coming; Matthew 26:64 says 'from now on' the Son of Man will be seen.
readings.objection: Some say this multiplies 'comings' to escape a difficulty; others ask why the same phrase means different events in nearby texts.

readings.reading: The coming is the Second Coming: the mission of Christ's followers to the Jewish people will continue, amid persecution, and will not be completed before the Son of Man returns. On this reading the verse is a promise of continuing mission to Israel, not a deadline.
readings.support: 10:17–22 broadens beyond the first tour to the whole age; Matthew's other uses of 'the Son of Man comes' point to the Parousia; Carson argues the saying assures continued opportunity in Israel until the end.
readings.objection: The word 'finish' (teleō) sounds like a time limit on a task, not open-ended continuation; preterists see this as reading in a long delay.

readings.reading: Many dispensationalists read the mission to Israel as interrupted by Israel's rejection of the King and resumed during the future Tribulation by Jewish witnesses (Revelation 7:1–8), who will not finish going through Israel's towns before Christ returns. Others favour a near reference to Jesus rejoining the disciples after their mission.
readings.support: The kingdom offer was to Israel first (10:5–6); the persecution described in 10:17–22 resembles Tribulation conditions in Matthew 24:9–14.
readings.objection: Critics object that the instructions were given to the Twelve in their own day, and that a gap of millennia in the middle of a single paragraph is hard to justify.

title: Some Standing Here Will Not Taste Death
summary: After calling disciples to take up the cross, Jesus says the Son of Man will come in his Father's glory with his angels and repay each person according to what he has done (16:27), and then that some standing there will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (16:28). Mark 9:1 and Luke 9:27 speak of seeing 'the kingdom of God' (Mark: 'come with power'); all three Gospels place the Transfiguration immediately after.
keyIssue: What did 'some' of the bystanders see before dying, and is verse 27 the same coming as verse 28?

readings.reading: Verse 28 refers to Christ's coming in judgment and kingdom vindication in AD 70, which 'some', not all, of the disciples lived to see. Many partial preterists (e.g. Gentry) distinguish verse 27, the final judgment of every person, from verse 28; others (e.g. DeMar) read both verses of AD 70, with 27 describing covenantal judgment on that generation.
readings.support: 'Some will not taste death' implies a span long enough that most bystanders would die, which suits roughly forty years better than six days; the wording matches 24:30–34 and 26:64.
readings.objection: Critics note that the Synoptic placement before the Transfiguration, and Peter's own appeal to the Transfiguration as eyewitness of Christ's 'power and coming' (2 Peter 1:16–18), point to a nearer fulfilment.

readings.reading: Verses 27 and 28 describe one event: the Son of Man came in glory with his angels, rendered judgment to each, and established his kingdom in AD 70, within the lifetime of some hearers. Because the repayment of 'each person' was then, the final judgment is past.
readings.support: The 'for' (gar) linking the verses and the unbroken flow from glory, angels and judgment to 'some standing here' are taken to forbid splitting them.
readings.objection: Treating the judgment of 'each person' as past places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy; critics also argue that 16:27 echoes the universal judgment of Psalm 62:12 and Romans 2:6. Proponents answer that the creeds cannot outrank Jesus's time limit.

readings.reading: The Transfiguration, six days later, is a preview and pledge of the Son of Man's kingdom glory, seen by Peter, James and John; it begins a series (resurrection, ascension, Pentecost, and arguably AD 70) by which Jesus's kingdom 'comes with power', all anticipating the final coming of 16:27.
readings.support: All three Synoptics attach the saying directly to the Transfiguration; Mark's version ('the kingdom of God come with power') fits Pentecost and the resurrection; 2 Peter 1:16–18 calls the Transfiguration a witness of Christ's 'power and coming'.
readings.objection: Preterists object that 'some will not taste death' is a strange way to describe an event six days away when none had died; amillennialists answer that the expression stresses privilege and certainty rather than delay.

readings.reading: The Transfiguration is a preview of Christ's future millennial kingdom glory: Peter, James and John saw in miniature the King coming in his kingdom, while 16:27 refers to the future Second Coming and judgment.
readings.support: 2 Peter 1:16–18 explicitly connects the Transfiguration to Christ's 'coming'; the immediate narrative sequence; Moses and Elijah suggest the kingdom with glorified and living saints.
readings.objection: Critics note the plural 'some' and 'not taste death' suggest a longer interval, and partial preterists argue the Transfiguration was a vision of glory, not a 'coming in his kingdom'.

readings.reading: The kingdom 'come with power' (Mark 9:1) refers to manifestations of God's reign within the disciples' lifetime, beginning with the Transfiguration and resurrection and especially Pentecost; the Parousia of 16:27 remains future and inaugurates the millennium.
readings.support: Ladd's already/not-yet: the kingdom is God's dynamic reign, which can 'come with power' before its consummation.
readings.objection: Preterists say this fails to explain the 'Son of Man coming' wording in Matthew; others see it as merging distinct events.

title: An Hour Is Coming When All in the Tombs Will Hear
summary: Jesus says the hour is coming and now is when the spiritually dead hear the Son's voice and live (5:25), then adds that an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (5:28–29), echoing Daniel 12:2.
keyIssue: Does 'an hour' teach a single general resurrection of righteous and wicked together, ruling out a thousand-year gap between two resurrections (Revelation 20:4–6)? And is the resurrection of 5:28–29 bodily and future, or fulfilled spiritually or corporately?

readings.reading: One general resurrection of all people, righteous and wicked, at Christ's return, followed by one final judgment. The 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:5 is the believer's present spiritual life with Christ or the soul's entrance into heaven, as 5:25 describes a present spiritual resurrection followed in 5:28–29 by a future bodily one.
readings.support: Both groups rise in the same 'hour' at the same voice; Daniel 12:2 and Acts 24:15 likewise speak of one resurrection 'of both the just and the unjust'; John 6:39–54 places believers' resurrection on 'the last day'.
readings.objection: Premillennialists reply that John's own 'hour' in 5:25 has already lasted two thousand years, so an 'hour' can span a millennium. Amillennialists answer that 5:25 is a spiritual hour by its nature, whereas 5:28–29 concerns a single bodily event at the last day.

readings.reading: Agrees with the amillennial reading: one bodily general resurrection and judgment at Christ's single return after the millennial period of gospel prosperity; 5:25 describes the spiritual resurrection by which the kingdom grows now.
readings.support: The two-stage pattern (spiritual resurrection now, bodily resurrection at the end) is how Augustine and the Reformed confessions understood Revelation 20 and John 5.
readings.objection: Premillennialists raise the same 'hour' objection; full preterists say the bodily-future reading ignores the near-coming context of John's eschatology.

readings.reading: Jesus speaks of the resurrection of both groups without specifying whether they occur together; as 'the hour' of 5:25 spans the whole church age, the 'hour' of 5:28 can contain both the resurrection of the righteous at Christ's return and the resurrection of the rest after the thousand years (Revelation 20:5).
readings.support: Revelation 20:4–6 explicitly separates a first resurrection of the blessed from 'the rest of the dead'; 1 Corinthians 15:23–24 lists an order ('each in his own order').
readings.objection: Amillennialists respond that John's Gospel consistently places the righteous's resurrection 'on the last day' (6:39–54), leaving no later day for the wicked to be raised.

readings.reading: There are distinct resurrections in sequence: of the church at the rapture, of Old Testament and Tribulation saints at Christ's return, and of the wicked after the millennium (Revelation 20:5, 11–15). John 5:28–29 describes the two kinds of resurrection, not their timing.
readings.support: Revelation 20 gives a thousand-year gap; 'the resurrection of life' and 'the resurrection of judgment' are qualitatively distinct, like the 'better resurrection' of Hebrews 11:35.
readings.objection: Critics say this multiplies resurrections beyond the text and conflicts with the single 'hour' and single 'last day' of John's Gospel.

readings.reading: The resurrection of 5:28–29 occurred in AD 70, when the dead were raised from Hades (the realm of the dead) into God's presence and the judgment took place; it was not the reanimation of physical corpses. Some, following Max King, see a corporate resurrection of the covenant people from the 'death' of the old covenant.
readings.support: Ties 5:28–29 to Daniel 12:2, whose fulfilment Daniel 12:7 places at the shattering of the holy people's power, which proponents identify with AD 70.
readings.objection: Denying a future bodily resurrection places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy (Nicene and Apostles' Creeds); Wright and others argue that 'resurrection' in Jewish and Christian usage meant bodily life after death, and 'all in the tombs' denotes bodies. Proponents answer that Hades-to-heaven language fulfils the text without physical bodies.

title: Will You Restore the Kingdom to Israel?
summary: The disciples ask the risen Jesus whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel. He replies that it is not for them to know the times or seasons the Father has fixed, but they will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and to the end of the earth. He is taken up and a cloud hides him; two men in white say this same Jesus will come in the same way as they saw him go.
keyIssue: Does Jesus affirm a future restoration of national Israel (only the timing is withheld), or redirect the question so that the kingdom is restored through the Spirit-empowered witness to the nations? And what does 'in the same way' imply about the manner of his return?

readings.reading: Jesus does not correct the disciples' expectation of a restored kingdom for Israel; he corrects only their curiosity about timing. The kingdom will be restored to Israel at his return, which will be personal, bodily and visible to the Mount of Olives (1:11–12; Zechariah 14:4), after the present church age of witness.
readings.support: After forty days of teaching about the kingdom (1:3), the apostles' question is assumed to be informed, not confused; 'times or seasons' implies there is a time; Acts 3:21 and Luke 22:29–30 keep Israel's restoration in view.
readings.objection: Covenant theologians respond that Jesus's answer replaces the national-political horizon with a universal one (1:8), and that the Spirit's coming, which the prophets tied to Israel's restoration (Isaiah 32:15; 49:6), is the beginning of that restoration.

readings.reading: Jesus redirects the question: Israel's restoration is being accomplished now as the Spirit is poured out and the witness goes from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, fulfilling Isaiah 49:6, where restoring Jacob and being a light to the nations are one task. The return 'in the same way' is Christ's personal, visible Second Coming at the end of the age.
readings.support: Acts 1:8 echoes Isaiah 49:6 and 32:15; Acts 15:16–18 interprets the rebuilt tent of David as the inclusion of Gentiles; the gathered remnant of Jews in Acts 2 is the restored Israel's nucleus.
readings.objection: Dispensationalists respond that this reads Isaiah selectively and that Jesus's answer would be misleading if the disciples' premise was wrong; amillennialists answer that Jesus regularly reframed questions (e.g. John 3:4).

readings.reading: The witness 'to the end of the earth' is the program by which Christ's kingdom expands until it fills the world; his return 'in the same way' is the final, bodily, visible Second Coming after that expansion. Postmillennial partial preterists such as Gentry insist that Acts 1:11 is not the AD 70 coming but the future Parousia.
readings.support: The parallel of ascension in a cloud and return in a cloud, the stress on 'this same Jesus', and the eyewitness emphasis ('as you saw him go') all point to a personal, visible return.
readings.objection: Amillennialists accept the bodily return but question the expected scale of success before it; full preterists object that the same 'cloud coming' language in the Gospels is applied to AD 70 by partial preterists themselves.

readings.reading: The return 'in the same way' means 'in a cloud', as the Old Testament describes the LORD coming in clouds of judgment; Christ returned in that manner in AD 70, discerned by faith rather than by physical sight. Restoration of the kingdom to Israel was the establishment of the new covenant people.
readings.support: Consistency with the AD 70 interpretation of 'coming on the clouds' in Matthew 24:30 and 26:64, which partial preterists themselves accept.
readings.objection: Critics argue that 'this same Jesus' and 'in the same way as you saw him go' stress a visible, bodily departure and return; denying a future bodily return places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

readings.reading: The church's mission and the Spirit's coming begin the restoration hope, while the bodily return of Christ will establish his reign on earth for the millennium; whether ethnic Israel has a special place in that reign is debated within the tradition.
readings.support: Keeps both the redirection of 1:8 and the literal return of 1:11, without requiring a pretribulational framework.
readings.objection: Dispensationalists see too little emphasis on Israel; amillennialists see no need for a millennium between the return and the new creation.

title: Times of Refreshing and the Restoration of All Things
summary: Peter calls the people of Jerusalem to repent so that their sins may be blotted out, 'times of refreshing' may come from the Lord's presence, and he may send the Christ appointed for them, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time of the restoration of all things (apokatastasis pantōn) spoken of by the prophets.
keyIssue: Is the 'restoration of all things' a millennial restoration of Israel's kingdom triggered by national repentance, the progressive subduing of Christ's enemies while he reigns from heaven, or the final new creation at his return?

readings.reading: Peter re-offers the kingdom to Israel: if the nation repents, Messiah will return and bring the restoration the prophets foretold, the millennial kingdom with Israel at its centre. Israel's rejection postponed this, and the restoration awaits national repentance at the end of the Tribulation.
readings.support: Acts 3:20 says Jesus was appointed 'for you' (Israel); 'restoration' echoes the disciples' question in Acts 1:6 (the verb apokathistēmi); the prophets' restoration oracles centre on Israel's land and kingdom.
readings.objection: Non-dispensationalists question whether the kingdom was 'offered' and 'postponed', and note that Peter immediately applies the promise to Abraham's blessing of 'all the families of the earth' (3:25–26).

readings.reading: The restoration of all things is the consummated new creation at Christ's return. Christ remains in heaven, reigning, until that day; when he comes, the restoration is complete. This leaves no room for an earthly millennial reign after his return before the final state.
readings.support: 'Heaven must receive him until' sets the Second Coming as the moment of restoration; Romans 8:19–23 and Revelation 21:5 ('I make all things new') describe the cosmic renewal the prophets foresaw (Isaiah 65:17).
readings.objection: Premillennialists respond that a millennium is the first stage of the restoration and the new creation its completion; postmillennialists stress that the restoration is in progress before the return.

readings.reading: Christ must stay in heaven until the restoration is accomplished: he rules from his throne now, subduing his enemies through the gospel (Psalm 110:1; 1 Corinthians 15:25), and returns only when that work has run its course. The passage thus implies that the restoration is a historical process brought to completion before the Second Coming.
readings.support: Psalm 110:1 ('sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool') and 1 Corinthians 15:24–26 together place the subduing of enemies during Christ's heavenly session, before his return.
readings.objection: Amillennialists answer that 'until the restoration' may mean 'until the time when restoration happens', at the return itself, not after a process; premillennialists say Psalm 110 does not specify the means of subjection.

readings.reading: The restoration begins at Christ's return with his reign over a renewed earth, the millennium, and is completed in the new heavens and new earth; repentance brings present 'refreshing' through the Spirit as a foretaste.
readings.support: Coheres with Acts 1:6 and Romans 11's hope for Israel without the postponement theory.
readings.objection: Amillennialists argue that the restoration of 'all things' at the return is total, not partial.

readings.reading: The restoration of all things was completed when the old covenant world passed and the new covenant order was fully established in AD 70; the 'times of refreshing' are the new covenant life now available in Christ.
readings.support: Peter speaks to his own generation; Jesus said Elijah 'restores all things' (Matthew 17:11) and connected the end with that generation.
readings.objection: Critics note the language of creation-wide restoration (Romans 8:21) has no clear fulfilment in AD 70, and the view's denial of a future return is outside the historic creeds.

title: Scoffers, Delay and New Heavens and Earth
summary: Peter warns that scoffers will come in the last days asking where the promise of Christ's coming is. He answers that as the world was once destroyed by water, so the present heavens and earth are stored up for fire; that with the Lord a day is as a thousand years; that the delay is patience; and that the day of the Lord will come like a thief, when the heavens pass away with a roar, the elements (stoicheia) dissolve with heat and the earth and its works 'will be found' (or 'burned up', a textual variant). Believers wait for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells.
keyIssue: Is this the final conflagration and renewal of the physical cosmos at the Second Coming, or covenantal language for the end of the old covenant order in AD 70? And does the fire annihilate creation or purge and renew it?

readings.reading: The final Day of the Lord at Christ's return, when the present cosmos is judged and purified by fire and renewed as the new heavens and new earth; the delay is God's patience during the whole age. Most Reformed amillennialists read 3:10 'will be found' (heurethēsetai) as laying bare for judgment, and the fire as purifying rather than annihilating.
readings.support: The parallel with the Flood (3:5–7), which judged but did not annihilate the world, points to cosmic renewal; Romans 8:21 and Revelation 21:1 confirm the hope; 'a thousand years as a day' assumes a long delay is possible.
readings.objection: Partial and full preterists argue that 'heavens and earth' can be covenantal-political language (Isaiah 51:15–16), and that stoicheia elsewhere means the elementary principles of the old order (Galatians 4:3, 9; Colossians 2:8, 20).

readings.reading: Many postmillennialists, including Gentry and Mathison, read 3:10–13 as the final consummation at Christ's single bodily return, after the long era of gospel advance; the 'delay' allows the gospel to prosper for a long age. Peter's appeal to creation and the Flood points to the material cosmos, not merely the Jewish order.
readings.support: Peter grounds his argument in the physical creation and the global Flood (3:5–6), and the new heavens and earth are a place 'where righteousness dwells', a consummate state (Isaiah 65:17 language here applied to its final form).
readings.objection: Other postmillennial preterists counter that the 'last days' and scoffers fit the generation before AD 70 (Matthew 24:48); Gentry answers that Peter's anticipating a long time span ('a thousand years as a day') points beyond that generation.

readings.reading: Some partial preterists (e.g. Leithart) read the passing 'heavens and earth' as the old covenant world, with its temple and elemental ordinances, dissolved in AD 70; the new heavens and new earth are the new covenant order. John Owen, in a sermon on 3:11, had already applied the dissolving heavens and earth to the Jewish church-state.
readings.support: Isaiah uses 'heavens and earth' for the covenant order (Isaiah 51:16; 65:17 is followed by a world still containing death, 65:20); 'the last days' (3:3) refers to the end of the old covenant age (Hebrews 1:2; 9:26); stoicheia means elementary religious principles elsewhere in Paul.
readings.objection: Other partial preterists, such as Gentry, reject this reading because Peter compares the coming judgment with the Flood and creation itself. Critics also note that the passage appears in a letter that expects a long delay, the opposite of the near-coming emphasis in Matthew 24.

readings.reading: The passage describes the passing of the old covenant world in AD 70; the new heavens and new earth of 3:13 are the new covenant realm in which righteousness dwells now, and there is no future cosmic conflagration.
readings.support: Don Preston argues that Peter's 'promise' comes from the prophets (3:2), whose new creation oracles (Isaiah 65–66) concerned Israel's covenant world, and that Jesus limited 'heaven and earth passing' to his generation (Matthew 24:34–35).
readings.objection: Critics, including partial preterists, argue that Peter's cosmic Flood analogy, the global judgment of 'the ungodly' and the scope of the new creation exceed AD 70; the view's denial of a future Second Coming and judgment places it outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

readings.reading: The Day of the Lord is an extended period beginning with the Tribulation and running through the millennium; the dissolution of the heavens and earth by fire comes at its end, after the millennium and the final judgment, preparing for the eternal state of Revelation 21.
readings.support: 'A day is as a thousand years' (3:8) is sometimes linked to the thousand-year span of the Day of the Lord; Revelation 20:11–21:1 places the passing of heaven and earth after the millennium.
readings.objection: Critics say that stretching 'the day' across a thousand years blurs Peter's point that the day comes suddenly, 'like a thief' (3:10).

readings.reading: The final conflagration and renewal follow the millennial reign of Christ and the last judgment; Peter does not mention the millennium because his concern is the certainty of the final day against scoffers.
readings.support: Fits the sequence of Revelation 20–21 while reading 2 Peter 3 as the final state.
readings.objection: Amillennialists argue that 2 Peter 3 links Christ's coming directly to the cosmic renewal, leaving no space for an intervening millennium.

title: Old Covenant Ready to Vanish Away
summary: After quoting Jeremiah 31:31–34 at length, the author says that by speaking of a 'new' covenant God has made the first obsolete, and what is becoming obsolete and growing old is near (engys) to disappearing.
keyIssue: If the old covenant was made obsolete at the cross, why is it still 'near to disappearing' when Hebrews is written? Does this point to the temple's destruction in AD 70 as the visible end of the old covenant order, and what follows for eschatology?

readings.reading: The old covenant was made obsolete in principle by Christ's death, but its institutions, the temple and sacrifices, were still standing and about to vanish; that happened in AD 70. Hebrews thus stands in a forty-year 'transition generation' between the old and new covenant eras, and it supports reading the 'last days' as the end of the old covenant age (Hebrews 1:2; 9:26).
readings.support: The present tense of the participles ('becoming obsolete and growing old') and engys ('near') imply an imminent historical event; the letter assumes the sacrifices still continue (10:1–3), and many date it before 70.
readings.objection: Some amillennialists respond that the verse may describe the inherent temporariness of the old order rather than predict AD 70. Preterists answer that the author's 'yet a little while' (10:37) and 'the Day drawing near' (10:25) supply the timeframe.

readings.reading: The covenant transition, begun at the cross, was completed only in AD 70, when the old covenant world passed; that moment was the arrival of the 'age to come', the resurrection and the Parousia (9:28). Since the old covenant vanished then, all eschatological promises tied to it were fulfilled then as well.
readings.support: The 'nearness' of 8:13 combined with 'he who is coming will come and will not delay' (10:37) and Christ appearing a 'second time' (9:28) are read as one event.
readings.objection: Critics accept that 8:13 points to AD 70 but deny that the end of the temple equals the bodily resurrection and final judgment; they note that Hebrews 9:27–28 links the second appearing to the judgment after death. The denial of a future return places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

readings.reading: The old covenant became obsolete with Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, and the passing of its shadows was sealed by the destruction of the temple. This does not end the age: the church lives in the 'last days' between Christ's first and second comings and awaits the city to come (13:14).
readings.support: Hebrews 9:9–10 calls the old system a symbol 'until the time of reformation'; Lane and others date Hebrews in the 60s and see 8:13 as alert to the temple's coming end.
readings.objection: Partial preterists press that the amillennial view underplays how much New Testament 'nearness' language is tied to AD 70; amillennialists answer that a near judgment does not exhaust the hope of the age to come.

readings.reading: The Mosaic covenant as a rule of life ended at the cross; the new covenant, made with Israel and Judah, is now applied spiritually to the church, but it will be fulfilled nationally with Israel at Christ's return. The obsolescence of the old covenant does not imply that God's promises to national Israel are cancelled.
readings.support: Jeremiah 31's new covenant is addressed to 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah'; progressive dispensationalists hold one new covenant with present (church) and future (Israel) phases.
readings.objection: Critics ask how this squares with a millennial temple and sacrifices (Ezekiel 40–48) after the old covenant has 'vanished'. Dispensationalists answer that millennial worship belongs to the new covenant, not a revival of the Mosaic covenant.

readings.reading: The decisive end of the old covenant in AD 70 vindicated Christ and cleared the stage for the new covenant kingdom to advance among the nations; the 'better covenant' (8:6) with its law written on hearts is the engine of the gospel's progressive success.
readings.support: Jeremiah 31:34 promises that 'all shall know me, from the least to the greatest', which postmillennialists take as an expanding reality as the new covenant spreads.
readings.objection: Amillennialists read 'all shall know me' as describing every member of the new covenant community, not an eventual majority of humankind.

title: Mount Zion and the Unshakable Kingdom
summary: Believers 'have come' not to Sinai but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to innumerable angels, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. God promises, quoting Haggai 2:6, 'yet once more' to shake not only the earth but heaven, removing what is shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain; since we are receiving (present participle) an unshakable kingdom, we should worship with reverence.
keyIssue: Is the 'shaking' of heaven and earth the end of the old covenant order in AD 70, the final cosmic judgment, or both? And how does the present 'have come to Zion' relate to future hope?

readings.reading: The 'shaking' that removes what is made is the dismantling of the old covenant order, climaxing in AD 70, while the church is already receiving the unshakable kingdom. Haggai 2:6–7 was originally about the shaking of nations and the glory of the latter temple, which the author sees fulfilled in the new covenant.
readings.support: 'Receiving' is present tense; 8:13 says the old order is near to disappearing; the contrast throughout chapter 12 is between Sinai and Zion, two covenants, not two cosmic eras.
readings.objection: Critics note that 12:26 says God will shake 'heaven' as well as earth, and that 12:27 speaks of removing 'created things', which suggests the final cosmic judgment. Partial preterists answer that the language is covenantal, as in the prophets.

readings.reading: An inaugurated eschatology: believers have already come to heavenly Zion, joined to the assembly in heaven, while the final shaking of heaven and earth at Christ's return will remove the present created order in its fallen form and leave the unshakable kingdom fully revealed. AD 70 may be a foreshadowing, but the 'yet once more' points to the consummation.
readings.support: 'Yet once more' (12:27) signals a final, once-for-all event; Hebrews elsewhere locates the believer's hope in a city 'to come' (13:14) and a 'second appearing' (9:28); Vos saw Hebrews as the classic expression of the 'already' heavenly participation.
readings.objection: Preterists argue that 'shaking' language in Haggai referred to historical upheaval among nations; amillennialists respond that Hebrews deliberately widens it to heaven and earth.

readings.reading: The present reception of the unshakable kingdom guarantees its triumph: what is shaken (the old order and every opposing power) is removed, while Christ's kingdom remains and advances until all is subject to him; the passage grounds confidence, not retreat.
readings.support: The removal of the old and the permanence of the new fit Daniel 2:44 (a kingdom that will never be destroyed) and Christ's present reign (Hebrews 1:13; 10:12–13, 'waiting until his enemies are made a footstool').
readings.objection: Amillennialists agree that the kingdom is unshakable but deny that this entails visible historical dominance before the end.

readings.reading: The heavenly Jerusalem is the present spiritual position of the church and the future dwelling of the saints (Revelation 21:2), distinct from the earthly Jerusalem of the millennium; the final shaking occurs at the end of the age, through the Tribulation judgments and the passing of heaven and earth. The passage does not replace Israel's earthly Zion promises.
readings.support: Hebrews speaks of a heavenly city, which dispensationalists distinguish from the earthly city promised to Israel (Zechariah 14; Isaiah 2).
readings.objection: Covenant theologians reply that the author contrasts the earthly Sinai with the heavenly Zion precisely to wean readers from earthly Jerusalem (13:12–14).

readings.reading: The shaking was entirely completed in AD 70; the unshakable kingdom fully came then, and believers now dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem with no further cosmic shaking to come.
readings.support: 'Yet a little while' (10:37) and the near disappearance of the old (8:13) fix the timeframe.
readings.objection: Critics object that the passage contrasts the created order with what is unshakable, a cosmic distinction that AD 70 did not effect; the denial of a future consummation places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

title: Perilous Times in the Last Days
summary: Paul tells Timothy that in the last days difficult (chalepoi) times will come: people will be lovers of self and money, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, lovers of pleasure rather than God, having a form of godliness but denying its power. 'Avoid such people', he adds (3:5); such teachers will 'not get very far', for their folly will be plain (3:9).
keyIssue: Is this a forecast of moral decline at the end of the church age, a description of the whole interadvent era, or a picture of the apostolic generation before AD 70? What does it imply for optimism or pessimism about history?

readings.reading: A prophecy of the moral and spiritual decline that will characterize the end of the church age, especially in professing Christendom, as part of the apostasy before the Lord's return (2 Thessalonians 2:3; 1 Timothy 4:1). Many see present cultural trends as a sign that the end is near.
readings.support: Paul's future tenses ('will come', 'will be'); parallels in Matthew 24:12 and Luke 18:8; the description of religious form without power fits an apostate church.
readings.objection: Critics note that Paul tells Timothy to avoid such people (3:5) and describes them as already present in Ephesus (3:6–8), which shows the 'last days' include Timothy's day. Dispensationalists reply that present instances foreshadow an intensified final form.

readings.reading: The 'last days' span the whole period from Christ's first coming to his return (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18); the vices Paul lists recur throughout church history and may intensify near the end, but they mark the age as a whole rather than one final phase. Believers face them with Scripture (3:14–17), not alarm.
readings.support: Paul applies the warning to Timothy's present ministry (3:5–9); Towner and others read the 'last days' as already under way in Ephesus.
readings.objection: Dispensationalists argue that the future tense points beyond Timothy's day; postmillennialists ask whether the amillennial reading leaves room for real cultural progress.

readings.reading: The 'last days' are the whole new covenant era, and Paul describes 'seasons' (kairoi) of difficulty within it, not unrelieved decline. Crucially, 3:9 says such people 'will not get very far' because their folly will be exposed: error is real but self-limiting, while the gospel advances.
readings.support: The plural kairoi suggests recurring periods; 3:9 limits the progress of evil; the context sends Timothy to preach the word, which equips for every good work (3:16–4:2).
readings.objection: Amillennialists and premillennialists see 3:13 ('evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse') as signalling persistent or growing evil; postmillennialists answer that 3:13 describes the impostors' own trajectory, not society's overall direction.

readings.reading: The 'last days' are the final days of the old covenant age, the forty years from the cross to AD 70; Paul warns Timothy about conditions in the church and society of his own generation, which climaxed in the apostasy and judgment Jesus foretold (Matthew 24:10–12).
readings.support: Paul instructs Timothy personally to avoid these people; the description matches the turmoil of the 60s; Hebrews 1:2 and 1 Peter 1:20 place the 'last times' in the apostolic era.
readings.objection: Amillennialists accept the present application but argue the last days continue until Christ's return (1 Corinthians 10:11; Hebrews 9:26 speaks of the 'end of the ages' as begun, not ended).

readings.reading: The last days began with Christ, and the vices of 3:1–5 will mark the whole age, culminating in a final apostasy and the Antichrist before Christ returns to establish his kingdom; the passage calls for vigilance throughout.
readings.support: Combines the present application (3:5–9) with the future intensification pointed to in 2 Thessalonians 2.
readings.objection: Postmillennialists object that this assumes a final decline the text does not require.

title: Things That Must Soon Take Place
summary: Revelation opens and closes with time markers: it reveals 'the things that must soon (en tachei) take place' (1:1; 22:6), 'the time is near' (engys, 1:3; 22:10), and John is told not to seal up the words of the prophecy (22:10), in contrast to Daniel, who was told to seal his vision because it concerned a distant time (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9). Jesus says 'I am coming soon' (22:7, 12, 20).
keyIssue: How should 'soon' and 'near' govern the interpretation of the book? They are the central texts for preterism, and every school must give an account of them.

readings.reading: The time markers are meant literally and frame the book: most of Revelation's prophecies (especially chs. 4–19) were fulfilled soon after writing, in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 and the Roman crisis around it. On the early date (c. 65–66) that most partial preterists hold, 'soon' meant within a few years. Chapters 20–22 extend to the present age and the final consummation.
readings.support: The markers stand at both ends of the book as bookends; the contrast with Daniel's sealing (Daniel 12:4) shows the time had arrived; the first readers were seven real churches promised blessing for heeding what was near (1:3).
readings.objection: Critics ask why the time texts should be strict for chapters 4–19 but not for 20–22, which also lie within the bracketing statements. Partial preterists answer that the book itself signals long-term developments (a 'thousand years', 20:2–7). The date of Revelation is also disputed (pre-70 vs c. 95).

readings.reading: Because the same time markers bracket the whole book, everything in it, including the Second Coming, resurrection, judgment and new creation of chs. 19–22, was fulfilled by AD 70. Consistency forbids splitting the book, as partial preterists do.
readings.support: Jesus says 'I am coming soon' in chapter 22 itself (22:7, 12, 20), right alongside the new Jerusalem visions; J. Stuart Russell's The Parousia pressed this consistency argument.
readings.objection: Critics reply that 'coming soon' language can describe impending comings in judgment within history (as in 2:5, 16) without being the final coming, and that the denial of a future bodily return and resurrection places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

readings.reading: 'En tachei' can mean 'quickly' or 'suddenly', describing the rapidity of the events when they begin, not their nearness; and 'near' is measured from God's perspective, for whom a thousand years is as a day (2 Peter 3:8). The events of chs. 4–22 lie mostly in the future, and the church is to live in imminent expectation.
readings.support: The same phrase en tachei is used of rapid action in Luke 18:8 and Acts 12:7; the New Testament treats the Lord's return as imminent yet not dated; the book's scope (global judgments, Satan's binding, new creation) exceeds any first-century event.
readings.objection: Preterists reply that 'near' (engys) is not a word about manner, and that a two-thousand-year delay strips the time markers of meaning for the first readers. Futurists answer that imminence is real: the next event on God's calendar could come at any time.

readings.reading: The prophecies began to be fulfilled soon after John wrote and then unfold in sequence through church history, from imperial Rome through the fall of the empire, the rise of the papacy and Islam, to the end; 'soon' refers to the beginning of the chain, which started in John's day.
readings.support: Accounts for the time markers without collapsing the book into one generation, and gives the book relevance to every era of history as a continuous prophecy.
readings.objection: Critics note that historicist schemes have disagreed widely and repeatedly had to be revised as predicted end dates passed, and that the first readers could hardly identify fulfilments centuries later.

readings.reading: 'Soon' expresses the inaugurated nature of the last days: with Christ's death and resurrection, the latter days of Daniel have begun (Revelation 1:1 echoes Daniel 2:28–29, replacing 'in the latter days' with 'soon'). The book's symbols describe the conflict of Christ and Satan throughout the whole age, every part of which is 'near' to the end.
readings.support: Beale notes that Revelation 1:1 alludes to Daniel 2 and changes 'latter days' to 'soon', implying that Daniel's kingdom prophecy has begun to be fulfilled; Hendriksen's 'progressive parallelism' reads each cycle as covering the whole age.
readings.objection: Preterists say this dissolves concrete time markers into a general nearness; futurists say it loses the book's prophetic specificity.

readings.reading: The book addressed real first-century crises and promised that the decisive events had begun, but its climax, Christ's coming, the millennium and the new creation, remains future; prophetic perspective telescopes near and far events, as the Old Testament prophets did.
readings.support: Ladd combined preterist and futurist elements: the beast of chapter 13 is both Rome and the end-time Antichrist.
readings.objection: Preterists see the telescoping theory as an escape; idealists see it as unnecessarily concrete.

title: The Beasts of Revelation 13 and the Number 666
summary: A beast with ten horns and seven heads rises from the sea; the dragon gives it his power and throne. One head seems mortally wounded but is healed, and the whole earth marvels. It blasphemes and makes war on the saints for forty-two months. A second beast, from the land, with lamb-like horns but a dragon's voice (later called the false prophet, 19:20), performs signs, causes an image of the first beast to be worshipped, and requires a mark on the right hand or forehead for buying and selling. The beast's number is 'the number of a man': 666 (13:18), though some ancient witnesses read 616.
keyIssue: Who or what is the beast: Nero and the Roman Empire, the papacy, a future Antichrist, or the persecuting state in every age? How does the number 666, and the variant 616, fit each view?

readings.reading: The sea beast is the Roman Empire and, as one of its heads, Nero Caesar, the first emperor to persecute Christians (AD 64–68), whose campaign lasted about forty-two months (late 64 to June 68). The number confirms it: spelled in Hebrew letters as nrwn qsr (Nero Caesar), the name totals 666 (50+200+6+50+100+60+200); in the Latin form Nero, without the final n (50), it totals 616, which explains the ancient variant. The land beast is a local power promoting emperor worship, variously the provincial imperial cult in Asia or (Chilton) Jerusalem's leadership collaborating with Rome.
readings.support: The spelling nrwn qsr is attested in an Aramaic document from Wadi Murabba'at (Hillers), and the 616 variant, known to Irenaeus and found in P115 (the oldest papyrus of Revelation 13) and Codex Ephraemi, is best explained by a scribe adjusting for the Latin spelling. Revelation calls the number one 'for one who has understanding' (13:18), a puzzle the first readers could solve. Bauckham, not a preterist, also accepts the Nero gematria.
readings.objection: Critics note that Irenaeus, who knew the 616 variant, never suggested Nero; that a Greek-speaking audience is asked to compute in Hebrew letters; and that the Hebrew form 'qsr' is a defective spelling. Proponents answer that John's Greek is full of Hebrew idiom (e.g. Abaddon, 9:11; Armageddon, 16:16), and that the Murabba'at text shows the spelling was in use.

readings.reading: The sea beast is the persecuting political power of every age, with Rome as John's present example; the land beast is false religion and propaganda that serves it. 666 is symbolic: six falls short of seven (completeness), so triple six signifies the beast's persistent failure to be divine despite its imitation of the Trinity. Many idealists allow that John may have used a Nero gematria as a pointer to the type.
readings.support: The dragon, sea beast and land beast form a parody of Father, Son and Spirit; the beast's 'death wound' parodies the slain Lamb (5:6; 13:3); John's numbers elsewhere are symbolic (7, 12, 144,000). Bauckham notes 666 is a triangular number (the sum of 1 to 36) and that 'beast' (thērion) spelled in Hebrew also totals 666.
readings.objection: Preterists argue that 'the number of a man' (13:18) calls for an individual identification; futurists say the symbolic reading empties the specific details (a mark, an image, a forty-two-month reign).

readings.reading: The sea beast is a future world ruler, the Antichrist, who heads a revived form of the Roman Empire (ten horns, Daniel 7:7–8, 24) and persecutes believers for the last three and a half years of Daniel's seventieth week. The healed head may be a literal recovery from apparent death or a revived empire; the land beast is a future religious leader; the mark is a literal means of economic control. The number will identify the man when he appears; past calculations have been premature.
readings.support: The beast's universal worship (13:8), its specific forty-two-month span matching Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, and its destruction at Christ's return (19:19–20) point to events not yet fulfilled; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–8 describes a future 'man of lawlessness'.
readings.objection: Preterists and idealists reply that John's first readers were told to calculate the number (13:18), which would be meaningless if it concerned someone two thousand years later; futurists answer that the instruction is addressed to all who read the prophecy, including the last generation.
