readings.reading: The sea beast is the papacy as a politico-religious power that arose from the fallen Roman Empire; the forty-two months are 1,260 years on the day-for-a-year principle (often dated 538–1798, from Justinian's era to the French capture of Pope Pius VI). The land beast is the papal hierarchy or, in some versions, a later power. 666 has been read as Lateinos (Greek for 'the Latin [man/kingdom]', 30+1+300+5+10+50+70+200 = 666), a suggestion first made by Irenaeus and favoured by Elliott; Adventist writers popularized the title 'Vicarius Filii Dei'.
readings.support: Reformers, the Westminster divines and many Protestant commentators read the beast as Rome's papal successor; Daniel 7's little horn rising after the fourth empire fits a power arising from Rome; the computation in Lateinos goes back to Irenaeus.
readings.objection: Critics note that 'Vicarius Filii Dei' is not an official papal title, that many different names can be made to total 666, and that the 1,260-year dates shift between historicist writers. Historicists answer that the convergence of the chronology with the history of papal temporal power is striking.

readings.reading: The beast is both Rome in John's day and the eschatological Antichrist in whom the persecuting power will culminate before Christ's return; Ladd saw Nero redivivus legends in the background and held that the fulfilment is still future. The number may allude to Nero as a type of the final Antichrist.
readings.support: Reflects how biblical prophecy often has a near historical referent and a future culmination (compare Antiochus Epiphanes in Daniel 11).
readings.objection: Preterists consider the future extension unnecessary; futurists consider the Roman reference too strong a concession.

readings.reading: Postmillennialists mostly follow the preterist identification of the beast with Nero and Rome: the beast was defeated in the first century, Christ's kingdom triumphed over imperial Rome, and the church need not fear a future world dictator. Others, such as James Jordan and Peter Leithart, propose alternative backgrounds for 666, notably the 666 talents of gold Solomon received yearly (1 Kings 10:14), which marks a king corrupted by wealth and power.
readings.support: The Solomonic reading fits the economic stress of 13:16–17 and the Old Testament background John uses everywhere; it is offered alongside or instead of the Nero calculation.
readings.objection: Critics of the Solomon reading note that 1 Kings 10:14 involves talents, not a man's name, whereas 13:18 calls it the number of a man and a name (13:17). Futurists add that a first-century fulfilment cannot account for the beast's final destruction at Christ's return (19:19–20).

title: The Harlot, the Seven Hills and the Seven Kings
summary: An angel shows John a woman, 'Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes', drunk with the blood of the saints, sitting on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. The angel explains that the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits and also seven kings: 'five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must remain a little while'; the beast that was and is not is an eighth, yet 'of the seven' (17:9–11). The ten horns are kings who later hate the harlot and burn her (17:16), and the woman is 'the great city that rules over the kings of the earth' (17:18).
keyIssue: Who is the harlot (Rome, Jerusalem, papal Rome, or a future system)? Do the seven kings let us date Revelation by identifying the king who 'is'? The date of Revelation is disputed: early (c. 65–68, before Jerusalem's fall) or late (c. 95, under Domitian, following Irenaeus).

readings.reading: The seven kings are Roman emperors counted from Julius Caesar, as Josephus, Suetonius and others counted: Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Gaius and Claudius have fallen; Nero (54–68) 'is'; Galba, who reigned only about seven months (68–69), is the one who 'remains a little while'. Revelation was therefore written under Nero, before AD 70. Many (Chilton, Gentry, Leithart) identify the harlot as apostate Jerusalem, allied with and riding on the Roman beast, which finally turned and destroyed her in AD 70 (17:16).
readings.support: Ancient historians (Josephus, Suetonius, Dio Cassius) count Julius as the first; the 'seven mountains' match Rome's famous seven hills, making the Roman reference explicit. Jerusalem is called the city where the Lord was crucified (11:8) and guilty of the blood of the prophets (Matthew 23:35–37; compare 18:24), and covenant infidelity is the prophets' meaning of 'harlot' (Ezekiel 16).
readings.objection: Late-date critics (e.g. Hitchcock) note that Augustus is often counted as the first emperor, that the city 'ruling over the kings of the earth' (17:18) is much more naturally Rome than Jerusalem, and that the external testimony of Irenaeus places Revelation under Domitian. Early-daters answer that Irenaeus's statement is ambiguous ('it was seen' may refer to John) and that internal evidence should prevail.

readings.reading: The seven heads are seven successive world empires that have oppressed God's people: commonly Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome (the one that 'is' in John's day), and a future revived Roman confederacy; the eighth is the Antichrist's kingdom. The harlot is a future apostate religious-economic system centred in a literal city (some say rebuilt Babylon, others Rome). John wrote c. 95 under Domitian.
readings.support: 'Mountains' are a common biblical symbol for kingdoms (Daniel 2:35; Jeremiah 51:25); the emperor-counting schemes are arbitrary because they must decide where to begin and whether to skip the three short reigns of 69; Irenaeus's testimony favours the late date.
readings.objection: Preterists respond that the angel explicitly explains the heads as the seven hills on which the woman sits, an unmistakable Roman landmark, and that 'kings' rather than 'kingdoms' is the angel's word; empire schemes also vary in their list.

readings.reading: The number seven is symbolic of completeness: the seven kings represent the whole series of anti-God world powers through history, with John's moment among them, near the end of the sequence. Babylon the harlot is the seductive world system of culture, commerce and false religion that tempts the church in every age, embodied in John's day by Rome.
readings.support: Revelation's numbers are consistently symbolic; the phrase 'he is an eighth and belongs to the seven' parodies Christ's resurrection; attempts to list emperors founder on which to count. Beale and Bauckham hold that the symbolic sense is primary, with Rome as the contemporary embodiment.
readings.objection: Preterists and futurists alike object that an angel's 'explanation' of the symbol (17:9–10) seems meant to give a concrete historical reference; idealists answer that the explanation itself is still in symbolic idiom ('this calls for a mind with wisdom').

readings.reading: The harlot is papal Rome, the seven-hilled city that became the seat of a corrupt church allied with the kings of Europe; the seven heads are successive forms of Roman government (kings, consuls, decemvirs, dictators, military tribunes, emperors, and then a further form), with the beast's final head the papal power. The burning of the harlot by the ten kings is the eventual turning of European powers against the papacy.
readings.support: The Reformers and Protestant commentators (e.g. Barnes, Elliott) found in Rome's seven hills, its persecution of the saints and its alliance with kings a precise match for papal Rome; this reading influenced confessions and Protestant culture for centuries.
readings.objection: Critics say the scheme reads European church history into a book addressed to first-century Asian churches, and that historicist schemes have produced conflicting lists of heads and dates.

readings.reading: Many amillennialists combine idealism with a primary Roman reference: Babylon is Rome as the embodiment of the world-city opposed to God, and the seven kings symbolize the full sequence of persecuting powers in history; the final beast (the eighth) points to the culminating Antichrist power before Christ's return. They generally hold the late date (c. 95).
readings.support: Holds together the clear Roman markers and the book's symbolic numerology; supports the cyclical structure of Revelation.
readings.objection: Early-daters argue that a symbolic seven cannot explain the precise 'five, one, and one for a little while' sequence; futurists argue that symbolism does not preclude a future literal city.

readings.reading: Like partial preterism, the beast and harlot are Rome and apostate Jerusalem and the date is pre-70; full preterists add that the destruction of the harlot in AD 70 was the climax of all biblical eschatology, after which the Second Coming, resurrection and new creation of chs. 19–22 were also fulfilled.
readings.support: Uses the same seven-kings count and Jerusalem identification as partial preterists, with the time texts of 1:1 and 22:10 applied to the whole book.
readings.objection: Critics accept the historical reading of chapter 17 but reject extending it to chs. 19–22; the view's denial of a future Second Coming places it outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

title: New Heaven, New Earth and the New Jerusalem
summary: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth have passed away and the sea is no more. The holy city, new Jerusalem, comes down from God like a bride, and a voice says that God's dwelling is with humanity; he will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning and pain will be no more (21:1–4). 'Behold, I am making all things new' (21:5). Outside are the cowardly, faithless and immoral, whose portion is the lake of fire (21:8). The river of the water of life flows from the throne, with the tree of life bearing fruit monthly and leaves for the healing of the nations; there is no more curse, and the servants see God's face and reign forever (22:1–5).
keyIssue: Is this the eternal state after the final judgment, a picture of the new covenant community already present in history, or both? Does the new creation replace or renew the present world? Why are there 'nations' needing 'healing' (22:2)?

readings.reading: The consummated new creation after Christ's return and the last judgment: the present world is renewed, not annihilated, and God dwells with his people forever. The new Jerusalem is the glorified church, the bride, in whom the promises of Eden, the temple and the land are fulfilled; aspects are already tasted now (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22), but the vision is of the final state.
readings.support: 21:4 promises the end of death, which 1 Corinthians 15:26 places at the end; 21:8 locates the wicked in the lake of fire after the judgment of 20:11–15; 'making all things new' renews existing creation (Romans 8:21).
readings.objection: Postmillennial preterists argue that the vision's present-tense invitations (22:17) and 'healing of the nations' imply historical, not purely eternal, application; amillennialists answer that the healing is a picture of complete wholeness, not ongoing disease.

readings.reading: Many postmillennial preterists (e.g. Chilton, Gentry) read the new Jerusalem as the new covenant church, already established after the old Jerusalem's fall, whose influence brings 'healing of the nations' through history; this present reality will be consummated in the eternal state after Christ's return. Others read the vision chiefly of the eternal state while affirming its historical foretastes.
readings.support: Isaiah 65:17–25, the source of 21:1, describes a new creation that still includes death at a great age (65:20), suggesting a historical process; Hebrews 12:22 says believers 'have come' to the heavenly Jerusalem; the gates are open to the kings of the earth bringing their glory (21:24–26).
readings.objection: Amillennialists and premillennialists object that 21:4 (no more death) cannot describe the present age; postmillennialists respond that the vision blends the present reality with its consummate fulfilment, as is common in prophecy.

readings.reading: The eternal state after the millennium and the great white throne judgment, in which the new Jerusalem descends to a re-created earth. Some dispensationalists (e.g. Pentecost) also hold that the new Jerusalem exists during the millennium as the dwelling of the resurrected saints, above or in relation to the earthly kingdom, and 21:9–22:5 may describe it in that role.
readings.support: The sequence of Revelation 19–21 (return, millennium, judgment, new creation) is read chronologically; the distinction between the earthly millennial Jerusalem and the heavenly new Jerusalem preserves both Israel's land promises and the church's heavenly hope.
readings.objection: Critics argue that the 'healing of the nations' and a city descending 'from heaven' are symbolic portraits of one final reality, and that a millennial new Jerusalem confuses the book's sequence.

readings.reading: The eternal state that follows Christ's millennial reign and the last judgment: a renewed earth, not a disembodied heaven, where God dwells with his people. The millennium is the first stage of Christ's victory on earth, and the new creation is its final stage.
readings.support: Ladd stressed the continuity between the present earth and the new earth, and the Old Testament hope of an earthly kingdom.
readings.objection: Amillennialists argue that once the new creation is admitted, a separate millennium becomes redundant.

readings.reading: The new heaven and new earth are the new covenant world established when the old covenant order (the 'first heaven and earth' and the 'sea' of the nations) passed away in AD 70; the new Jerusalem is the church, now dwelling with God, and its open gates (22:17) invite the nations today. There is no future cosmic renewal.
readings.support: The book's time markers (22:6, 10, 12) are placed right after the new creation vision; Isaiah 65:20 shows a 'new heavens and earth' that still includes death, and 22:15 shows sinners still outside the city.
readings.objection: Critics reply that 21:4 promises the end of death, mourning and pain, which have not ceased; that 21:8 places the wicked in the lake of fire; and that the denial of a future bodily resurrection and new creation places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

readings.reading: A symbolic portrait of the perfected people of God and their final fellowship with him, drawn from Eden, Ezekiel's temple and Isaiah's new creation. The cube-shaped city (21:16) recalls the Holy of Holies, so the whole community is God's sanctuary.
readings.support: Beale shows how the city is a temple-garden fulfilling Ezekiel 40–48 and Genesis 2; the descriptive details (gold like glass, pearl gates) are visionary.
readings.objection: Some ask whether the symbolic reading loses the physicality of the new creation; idealists answer that the symbols point to a real, embodied future.
